newsitem.title: DUBAI: GOLF-OLAZABAL BACK WITH REALISTIC TARGETS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-OLAZABAL BACK WITH REALISTIC TARGETS.

text.p: Jose Maria Olazabal returns to competitive golf this week following 18 months of chronic foot problems which at times left him barely able to walk with a realistic approach to his prospects.
After being reduced to a spectator's role a year ago, he is sensibly refusing to set targets at the Dubai Desert Classic where his comeback will begin on Thursday.
"I want to play well...but I have to be realistic. After 18 months without competition, it would be a little strange to do well," he said at the Emirates Course on Tuesday.

"At one stage I looked at the chance of not playing again so just being here is a blessing. But my game is not very sharp at the moment and my main aim this first week is to try my feet and see how I cope with the demands of a tournament on a daily basis.
"I'm not setting any targets or playing schedules. My main concern right now is to forget what happened for 18 months and concentrate on improving the situation in my feet.
"I have to concentrate on what I have to do over the next few weeks and get ready to play good golf as soon as possible," he said.

The 31-year-old Spaniard struggled through increasing foot problems during 1995, the year after he captured the U.S. Masters title, and they finally caught up with him at the Lancome Trophy in September.
Though he placed a respectable 26th, he was in so much discomfort that he withdrew from the Ryder Cup team for which he had been awarded a wild card spot just 10 days earlier.
So began his lengthy absence from the sport. He planned comebacks several times during 1996 only to abort them at the last minute because he was not confident of lasting one round, let alone four.
He was diagnosed three times as suffering from rheumatoid arthritis in both feet but various courses of treatment failed to alleviate the situation.
A chance meeting with a German doctor last autumn, when he went to Germany to have some golf shoes adjusted, led to a reassessment of his problem.
The doctor, Hans-Wilhelm Muller-Wohlfahrt, diagnosed a bio-mechanical problem and put Olazabal on a new course of exercise and physiotherapy.

"Before that I was doing nothing at all, sitting at home watching television or listening to music. Since then everything has improved without setbacks, though I am not yet 100 per cent. There is still a little pain towards the end of rounds.
"But compared to how it was before, it is much better. It is a bearable pain."
"You have good days and bad days," he said, adding that not being able to walk from his bed or stand for more than 15 minutes because of the pain were perhaps the lowest points.
"But even when you are not feeling too bad, it goes through your mind that you are not playing golf and that is bad, too.
"It's been very hard. Watching golf on television when you realise you may never play again -- perhaps that was the hardest part."
Olazabal was dismissive of false reports last year that he was suffering from AIDS, cancer or obesity.
He said that depending on how he performed this week he hoped to play a few more events in Europe before going to the U.S. Masters at Augusta in April.
"My intention is to play the Masters if all goes well but I will have to see how strong I feel and how good I feel after this week," he said.

He has set himself a testing week, playing full practice rounds on Monday and Tuesday, the pro-am on Wednesday before the event itself beginning on Thursday, seven successive days if he makes the halfway cut.

He said there was no guarantee the problem would not return but he intended to think positively. "I believe it will improve so that I will be able to play normally. I think positive thinking helps everyone."
